narrative.text: The title page of a Persian translation, by staff of Tabriz University of Medical Sciences' nursing and midwifery faculty, of WHO guidelines on screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention; the extracted Persian text is partly garbled.
A second title page of the Persian translation of WHO's cervical precancer screening and treatment guidelines, naming Tabriz University of Medical Sciences; the text is partly garbled.

A publication details page for the Persian translation of WHO's 2013 cervical precancer screening and treatment guidelines, stating that translation rights were granted to Tabriz University of Medical Sciences and naming the translators and editors; the extracted Persian text is largely garbled by font encoding.

The translators' preface, which appears to note that cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide and gives figures on deaths in 2012 and incidence in Iran. The extracted Persian text is badly garbled by font encoding, so only figures and some words can be read.

The table of contents of the Persian guideline translation, listing sections on methods, recommendations, research gaps and dissemination; the Persian text is garbled by font encoding and only page numbers are clear.

Continues the table of contents, listing annexes with flowcharts for screen-and-treat strategies using HPV testing, VIA or cytology with cryotherapy or LEEP, for women of negative, unknown or positive HIV status. The Persian text is garbled, with English terms and a WHO web address legible.

Lists WHO staff from headquarters and regional offices and external experts who contributed to the cervical precancer guidelines; names and affiliations are in English while the Persian headings are garbled.
Continues the list of guideline contributors, naming experts from institutions such as the CDC, IARC, PATH, Jhpiego and McGill University.
Continues the list of guideline contributors and external reviewers from countries including Spain, France, India, Kenya, Peru and the United States.
Ends the list of contributors with external reviewers from Germany, Italy, Bhutan, France, Belgium and the United Kingdom.

Describes how declarations of interests were managed and the roles of the technical groups, including the External Review Group convened in 2010 and the guideline development and methods groups in 2011. It appears to note that the guidelines do not address HPV vaccination; the Persian text is largely garbled by encoding.

The acknowledgements of the guidelines, thanking the methods group, McMaster University staff and funders including the Flanders International Cooperation Agency, France's INCa and the GAVI Alliance; the Persian text is garbled.
A list of abbreviations used in the guidelines, such as CIN, HPV, LEEP, VIA, GRADE and PICO, given in English with a garbled Persian heading.

The executive summary of the Persian guideline translation, explaining CIN grades and the screen-and-treat approach as an alternative to cytology, colposcopy and biopsy. It lists HPV testing, VIA and cytology as screening tests and cryotherapy, LEEP and cold knife conization as treatments, with flowcharts in annexes for women by HIV status; the Persian text is largely garbled.

Summarizes, in garbled Persian, how the guidelines were developed using WHO's handbook, a guideline development group, management of interests and systematic reviews of test accuracy and treatment effects. It also mentions research priorities such as sequential testing strategies and outcomes in women with HIV.

Gives the summary screen-and-treat recommendations, which apply to all women regardless of HIV status. They advise against cold knife conization and favour HPV testing over VIA, or VIA where resources are limited, followed by cryotherapy or LEEP. The Persian text is garbled by font encoding.

Presents a decision flowchart helping programme managers choose among screen-and-treat strategies based on resources, such as HPV testing alone, VIA alone or sequential testing; the Persian text is garbled.

The introduction to the guidelines, explaining that CIN2+ can progress to cervical cancer, that 1–2% of women have CIN2+ each year, with higher rates among women with HIV, and that standard cytology-based screening demands considerable resources. The Persian text is largely garbled by encoding, with some English footnotes legible.

Continues the introduction, listing treatments for CIN such as cryotherapy, LEEP/LLETZ and cold knife conization and noting that the guidelines build on other WHO cryotherapy and treatment guidance. It explains the screen-and-treat strategies considered; the Persian text is garbled, with English footnotes legible.

Notes that recommendations rest on evidence of test accuracy and treatment benefits and harms, and identifies the intended audience of policy-makers, managers and reproductive health and HIV programme staff. It also describes the GRADE evidence-to-recommendation tables; the Persian text is garbled.

Describes the guideline methods, following WHO's handbook, including a 17-member guideline development group chaired by Joanna Cain and a 33-member external review group of practitioners and researchers. It also mentions online surveys used to rank outcomes; the Persian text is garbled.

Explains how members rated outcomes on a 1–7 scale, with those averaging 4 or above included in the evidence review. Table 1 lists the priority questions comparing screen-and-treat strategies using HPV testing, VIA and cytology with or without colposcopy; the Persian text is garbled.

Describes how evidence was synthesized, noting that randomized trials comparing complete screen-and-treat strategies were scarce, so test accuracy studies were combined with treatment effect data and modelled outcomes. It describes eligibility criteria including women of varying HIV status and PRISMA reporting; the Persian text is garbled.

Describes data extraction, quality assessment with QUADAS and meta-analysis in Stata 12 for test accuracy, and Table 2 lists critical outcomes such as cervical cancer deaths. It notes that evidence was presented in GRADE profiles for each recommendation; the Persian text is garbled by font encoding.

A page from the Persian edition of WHO's guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention, describing the methods: modelled outcomes for screen-and-treat strategies, evidence profiles and GRADE ratings of evidence quality as high, moderate, low or very low, and evidence-to-recommendation tables. It mentions a meeting of the guideline groups in April 2012 to formulate recommendations; the extracted Persian text is badly garbled by a font-encoding problem, leaving mainly Latin terms such as GRADE and false/true positive legible.

Describes, as far as the garbled Persian extraction allows, how the guideline group and methods group ran the recommendation meeting with experts from many disciplines and regions, presenting evidence profiles on benefits, harms, values, preferences and resources. It notes that the group agreed the evidence could apply to all recommendations and explains the meaning of recommendation strength, with many recommendations being conditional. The extracted text suffers from a character-encoding fault and is only partly legible.

Outlines, in garbled Persian text, how WHO guideline groups reviewed questions and systematic review protocols before and during guideline development and how recommendations apply to individuals and policy-makers. The extraction has a font-encoding problem, so only fragments such as WHO, GDG and ERG are clearly legible.

Introduces the chapter of recommendations to help programme managers choose a screen-and-treat strategy, pointing to a decision flowchart and to strategy flowcharts for women of negative or unknown HIV status and for HIV-positive women. It begins considerations on the screening tests covered, HPV testing, cytology and VIA; the Persian text is garbled by an encoding fault, with mostly technical terms legible.

Continues the screening considerations, noting that VIA is suited to women whose transformation zone is visible, usually under age 50, and sets out treatment considerations with cryotherapy as first choice and LEEP when women are not eligible. It gives screening intervals, such as rescreening after at least five years after a negative HPV test and follow-up one year after treatment; the extracted Persian is largely garbled by a font-encoding problem.

Gives rescreening intervals for HIV-positive women or women of unknown status in high-HIV settings, within three years after a negative test, and follow-up one year after treatment, referring to the relevant flowchart annexes. It then begins a recommendation on screening with an HPV test followed by cryotherapy or LEEP versus VIA-based screening; the Persian extraction is garbled by an encoding fault.

Adds that where resources are limited and HPV testing is not feasible, the panel suggests screening with VIA and treating with cryotherapy or LEEP, with remarks that HPV-based screening brings greater reductions in cancer and deaths and that cytology programmes need substantial resources for quality control, training and colposcopy. The Persian text is garbled by a font-encoding fault, and the content is inferred from the partly legible wording and technical terms.

Discusses the comparison between HPV testing and cytology followed by colposcopy where quality cytology programmes exist, noting that either may be used. It summarizes evidence, rated low quality because few studies compared the diagnostic accuracy of the test sequences, and explains that the cytology–colposcopy strategy was modelled in two scenarios. The extracted Persian is largely garbled by a font-encoding problem.

Explains the two modelled scenarios for cytology followed by colposcopy, treatment based on colposcopy findings alone or after biopsy, and reports that differences in CIN2+ recurrence, cervical cancer and deaths between strategies may be small. It also discusses differences in overtreatment and related harms. The Persian text is garbled by an encoding fault, with figures and Latin terms the most legible parts.

Compares estimated outcomes of HPV testing with or without colposcopy follow-up, such as more biopsies and complications, and introduces a recommendation on screening with an HPV test followed by VIA and treatment with cryotherapy or LEEP. It notes that this approach may detect slightly more cancers and lead to fewer unnecessary treatments than HPV testing alone; the Persian extraction is garbled by a font-encoding fault.

Reports that HPV testing followed by VIA leads to fewer women being overtreated, saving resources, and explains the modelled results for HIV-positive women, where benefits and harms may differ, with estimates of CIN2+ recurrence, cancer and deaths. It also compares outcomes of VIA alone, including higher overtreatment due to more false positives. The Persian text is garbled by an encoding problem.

Notes that overtreatment and complications may be greater with VIA alone, with similar results for HIV-positive women, and presents a recommendation suggesting HPV testing followed by VIA over cytology followed by colposcopy. It adds that the benefits of the two strategies are similar but reductions in cancer and death may be slightly greater with HPV testing and colposcopy; the extracted Persian is largely garbled by a font-encoding fault.

States that the panel judged the benefits of each strategy to outweigh harms and costs, though cost differences are uncertain and colposcopy demands more trained staff, quality control and time and may lead to more loss to follow-up. It notes the recommendation applies regardless of HIV status and that few trials or studies assessed test sequences or accuracy in HIV-positive women. The Persian extraction is garbled by a character-encoding problem.

Discusses concerns about cytology programmes in settings with weak health systems or limited resources, noting that quality assurance needs more resources than other strategies and that slow results risk loss to follow-up. It also notes the absence of studies on eligibility for cryotherapy and the group's distinction between treating based on colposcopy findings versus biopsy; the Persian text is garbled by a font-encoding fault, apart from a PICO footnote.

Explains, in garbled Persian, that in some studies only women with positive colposcopy or biopsy results were treated, so test sequences were not directly evaluated and modelling was used. It notes that other benefits of screening, such as detecting sexually transmitted infections, were raised but not measured. The extraction suffers from a font-encoding fault.

Describes dissemination of the guidelines online through WHO's library database, reproductive health web page and the Reproductive Health Library, and through HRP publications reaching over 2,000 subscribers and partner organizations. The Persian text is largely garbled by an encoding problem, but the English footnotes with web addresses are legible.

Notes that the guidelines are initially available in English, with translations dependent on funding and encouraged by interested parties, and describes evaluation through download counts. It anticipates enough new evidence to update the recommendations about five years after publication; the Persian text is garbled by a font-encoding fault.
The first page of the reference list, citing studies and WHO handbooks on HPV testing, HIV-positive women and guideline development.
Continues the reference list, citing the Cochrane handbook, GRADE papers and WHO cervical cancer costing tools.

Annex 1, declarations of interest, stating in partly garbled Persian that 15 of 54 experts declared interests related to cervical cancer, summarized in English. It lists individual declarations, such as Marc Arbyn's research funding and role with a European research organisation, and grants received by various experts from manufacturers and agencies. It notes that funders had no role in data collection, analysis or interpretation.

Continues the English declarations of interest, such as Eduardo Franco's advisory roles and honoraria from Merck, Roche and Gen-Probe and other experts' links to HPV test and vaccine studies. It also describes PATH studies that used donated vaccines and careHPV tests from Merck, GSK and Qiagen.

Annex 2, the decision-making flowchart for choosing a screen-and-treat strategy at programme level, guiding managers through questions on resources and existing cytology programmes. Most of the Persian is garbled by an encoding fault, but legible fragments show that HPV testing or cytology followed by colposcopy, with cryotherapy or LEEP, may form the programme.

A note, in garbled Persian, explaining that each shaded box refers to a strategy flowchart in Annex 3 for HIV-negative or unknown-status women or Annex 4 for HIV-positive women or those in high-HIV settings.

Annex 3 opens the strategy flowcharts for women of negative or unknown HIV status, noting that they do not indicate which strategy is preferred and pointing to the Chapter 3 recommendations; the Persian text is garbled by an encoding fault.

A flowchart for screening with an HPV test and treating with cryotherapy, or LEEP when ineligible, using VIA to check eligibility, with referral of suspected cancer and follow-up after one year; most text is garbled but the flowchart labels are legible.
A note, in garbled Persian, referring readers to the Chapter 3 recommendations for guidance on which strategy is recommended and factors to consider.

A flowchart for screening with an HPV test followed by VIA, with treatment by cryotherapy or LEEP only when both are positive, follow-up after one year and rescreening after at least five years if negative; much of the Persian is garbled.
A repeated note, in garbled Persian, referring readers to the Chapter 3 recommendations when choosing a screen-and-treat strategy.

A flowchart for screening with VIA and treating with cryotherapy, or LEEP when ineligible, with referral of suspected cancer and follow-up one year after treatment; the main text is garbled but the flowchart labels are legible.

A flowchart for screening with an HPV test followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, and treatment with cryotherapy or LEEP if CIN2+ is found, or rescreening within three years if CIN1 or less; the Persian text is partly garbled.
A repeated note, in garbled Persian, pointing readers to the Chapter 3 recommendations for guidance on strategy choice.

A flowchart for screening with cytology followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, and treatment with cryotherapy or LEEP if CIN2+ is confirmed, with follow-up after one year and rescreening within three years otherwise. The Persian text is garbled by an encoding fault apart from the flowchart labels.

Annex 4 opens the flowcharts for HIV-positive women or women of unknown status in high-HIV settings, starting with HPV testing and treatment with cryotherapy, or LEEP if ineligible, rescreening within three years and follow-up after one year. The extracted Persian is garbled by a different encoding fault from earlier pages.
A note, in garbled Persian, referring readers to the Chapter 3 recommendations for guidance on which strategy is recommended.

A flowchart for HIV-positive women for screening with an HPV test followed by VIA, treating with cryotherapy or LEEP only when both tests are positive and following up one year after treatment. The Persian text is garbled by a font-encoding problem.

A flowchart for HIV-positive women for screening with VIA and treating with cryotherapy or LEEP when ineligible, with referral for suspected cancer and follow-up after one year. The Persian text is garbled by a font-encoding fault.

A flowchart for HIV-positive women for screening with an HPV test followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, treating CIN2+ with cryotherapy or LEEP and rescreening within one year if CIN1 or less. The Persian text is garbled by an encoding fault.

A flowchart for HIV-positive women for screening with cytology followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, treating CIN2+ with cryotherapy or LEEP and rescreening within three years if CIN1 or less. The Persian text is largely garbled apart from the final labels.

Annex 5, the search strategies used to review evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing, VIA, cytology and colposcopy, listing OVID MEDLINE search terms up to 2012. It also mentions searches of EMBASE, the Cochrane Library and LILACS, with Persian headings garbled by an encoding fault.
Continues the search strategies, giving the EMBASE and OVID MEDLINE search terms for colposcopy accuracy up to September 2012; the Persian headings are garbled.

Annex 6, a PRISMA flow diagram of studies identified, screened and included in the review of diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing, VIA, cytology and colposcopy, with study counts at each stage. The Persian text is partly garbled by an encoding fault.
Annex 7, a list of the studies included in the diagnostic accuracy review of cervical screening tests, citing mainly comparative studies of HPV testing, VIA and Pap smears from various countries.
Continues the list of included diagnostic accuracy studies, citing work on VIA versus Pap smear, HPV testing in routine screening and screening of HIV-infected women in China.
The back cover bearing the English title of the WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention.
